target_customer: Public and private hospitals and governments in South Asia that adopt the program, funded by philanthropy; beneficiaries are patients and family caregivers
problem: Patients leave hospitals with families unprepared to care for them, causing avoidable complications and readmissions.
business_model: Nonprofit funded by grants and philanthropy; trains nurses who teach family caregivers inside existing health systems

founders.name: Edith Elliott
founders.background_notes: YC page lists her as Founder/CEO. Later titled co-founder and co-CEO.

founders.name: Shahed Alam
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder in InfluenceWatch and TED 2022 coverage, not on the YC page.

founders.name: Katy Ashe
founders.background_notes: The YC blog post titled Female founder stories: Edith Elliott and Katy Ashe, founders of Noora Health (YC W14) names her as a founder.

investors: MacKenzie Scott and Dan Jewett (20M gift within the total)

technical_complexity.rationale: Mostly program design, training content and later software for hospitals; the difficulty was operational and clinical adoption, not technology.

defensibility.rationale: Embedding in government hospital systems and state partnerships is slow to replicate, and outcome data builds credibility.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No for-profit incumbent targeted the wedge; it is a nonprofit so takeover is not a factor.

market_need_then: Hospitals in India discharged patients with little family training; the 2014 pilot at Narayana Hospital in Bangalore tested cardiac patient training, and TechCrunch covered it in March 2014.

branding.community_and_virality: TED talk by the founders and recognition from Skoll and the Audacious Project.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong philanthropic recognition (TED stage, Skoll award) and a named flagship program, but limited consumer brand reach.

outcome_analysis: Noora Health grew from a 2014 Bangalore pilot into a nonprofit operating across India, Bangladesh, Indonesia and Nepal, with reported reach of tens of millions of caregivers and a 52 million dollar award package in April 2022 from the Audacious Project and Skoll Foundation. Success rests on measured clinical outcomes and government partnerships, though reported outcome figures vary by source and some are not peer reviewed.
notes: Nonprofit, so there are no equity rounds. InfluenceWatch says YC gave training and about 120K seed funding; not recorded as a round. The 52M total combines two awards and the Audacious Project grantee page lists the cohort as 2021 while Business Wire says April 2022. CB Insights shows a conflicting total of 60K. People trained figures conflict across pages (30M, 51M, 58M, 65M). No dated 2014 competitor source was found.
